```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.align = "center", dpi = 72)
library(tidyverse)
```

## Fancy Histograms!

We'll start by making some histograms.

```{r}
#install.packages("dslabs")
library(dslabs) 

data(heights)
glimpse(heights)
```

This data is the heights of humans, divided by their biological sex.

Use ggplot to make a histogram of all of the heights:

```{r warning=F, message=FALSE}
heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height)) + geom_histogram() + labs(title = "human heights")

```

Change up the binwidth and see how the plots change. Try 1, 5, 10, and 20

```{r}
bw <- 1
heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = bw) + labs(title = "human heights", subtitle = paste("binwidth of ", bw))

# if you're interested in looping in R
for (bw in c(1, 5, 10, 20)) {
p <- heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = bw) + labs(title = "human heights", subtitle = paste("binwidth of ", bw))
print(p)
}

```

Smooth this out to an empirical density with `geom_density()`

```{r}
heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height)) + geom_density() + labs(title = "human heights")
```

Use a new argument in the `aes()`, `group =` to split this density by sex

```{r}
heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height)) + geom_density(mapping = aes(group = sex)) + labs(title = "human heights")

```

OR we can do it with `color` or `fill.` If you say you want to color by sex, R knows that you want a different curve for each of them.

```{r}
heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height, color = sex)) + geom_density() + labs(title = "human heights")

heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height, fill = sex)) + geom_density() + labs(title = "human heights")

heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height, color = sex, fill = sex)) + geom_density() + labs(title = "human heights")
# honestly kinda my favorite cause it removes those outlines
```

If you've used fill, then there is now a slight issue that they are overlapped. We can fix this with alpha transparency!

```{r}
heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height, color = sex, fill = sex)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + labs(title = "human heights")

```

Let's make some boxplots of the same information.

```{r}
## all heights (no sex split)
heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(title = "human heights")

## including the sec needs a y! 
heights |> ggplot(aes(x = height, y = sex, fill = sex)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(title = "human heights", subtitle = "divided by sex")

```

## Quantatitive summaries:  

Find the mean and median overall. 

```{r}
heights |> summarise(mean_height = mean(height), 
                     median_height = median(height))
```

Find the mean and median for both groups. 

```{r}
heights |> group_by(sex) |> 
  summarise(mean_height = mean(height), 
            median_height = median(height))

## OR 
# the "new way"

heights |> summarise(mean_height = mean(height), 
                     median_height = median(height), 
                    .by = sex)

```

How tall is the tallest woman? How short is the shortest man? 

```{R}
heights |> 
  group_by(sex) |> 
  summarise(min_height_by_sex = min(height), 
            max_height_by_sex = max(height))

## or 
heights |> 
  filter(sex == "Male") |> 
  slice_min(height)


## or this nieche things
bind_rows(list(
      heights |> filter(sex == "Female") |> slice_max(height), 
      heights |> filter(sex == "Male") |> slice_min(height)
      )
    )

```

Use your summary table and pipe it to a ggplot to make a bar graph showing the mean of both groups. 

```{R }
heights |> 
  group_by(sex) |> 
  summarise(mean_height = mean(height), 
            median_height = median(height))|> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = mean_height)) + 
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Mean heights for each sex")
```

## Layering plots!

Penguins!

```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
glimpse(penguins)
```

We can use boxplots to visualize the distribution of weight (body_mass_g) within each species:

```{r}
penguins |> 
  drop_na(body_mass_g) |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = body_mass_g, x = species)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Body mass by species")

```

What if we also want the points? Layering!! Add a geom_point to your existing boxplot. geom_boxplot + geom_point!

```{r}
penguins |> 
  drop_na(body_mass_g) |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = body_mass_g, x = species)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Body mass by species")

```

But, these are all stacked up... to actually see them, use "geom_jitter" instead of points

```{r}
## original flavor of jitter spans the whole space
penguins |> drop_na(body_mass_g) |> ggplot(aes(y = body_mass_g, x = species)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter() + labs(title = "Boxplot of Mass by Species", subtitle = "added jittered points")

## you can squash the points in with "width =" 
## default is 40% of the resolution of the data
## (you can also change height, but that's not relevant here)
penguins |> drop_na(body_mass_g) |> ggplot(aes(y = body_mass_g, x = species)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter(width = 0.2)  + labs(title = "Boxplot of Mass by Species", subtitle = "added jittered points with less width")

```

How to get the boxplots on top? The layers are plotted in the order you give them, so change the ordering to geom_point + geom_boxplot. (You might want to change the alpha on the boxplot to be able to see the plots under them)

```{r}
penguins |> 
  drop_na(body_mass_g) |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = body_mass_g, x = species)) + 
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Mass by Species", 
       subtitle = "added jittered points with less width")

```

Maybe let's try replacing the boxplot with a `geom_violin()`?

```{r}
penguins |> 
  drop_na(body_mass_g) |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = body_mass_g, x = species)) + 
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2) + 
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(title = "Violin of Mass by Species", 
       subtitle = "added jittered points with less width")


```

## Presidental Elections Data

```{r}
# install.packages("pscl")
library(pscl) # loads in the package that has this data. 
## You might need to install this...

# data for presidental elections
votedata <-  presidentialElections
glimpse(votedata)
```

Let's look at the democratic vote by state for 2000. We can't use `geom_bar` for a bar chart, since we have the category in one variable and the "height" of the bar in another. We need `geom_col()`

Make a bar graph of the democratic vote by state in 2000. 

```{r}
votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2000) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = state, y = demVote)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2000 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)")


```

Well this looks awful. We have two options: swap the x and y or the more fun sounding... Coordinate flip! 

Use `coord_flip()` on the previous graph to make it better. 

```{r fig.height=7, fig.width=5}

votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2000) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = state, y = demVote)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2000 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)")

```

I don't love the squashed together coordinates, but it's a display window issue.

So. This is a helpful graph, but it would be *more* helpful if it was ordered. 
Use `x = reorder(x_variable, y_variable)` in `aes()` to order the x variable by the y variable

```{r fig.height=7, fig.width=5}
# i added the code chunks post-publishing the template to fix this squashed graph too

votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2000) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(state, demVote), y = demVote)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2000 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)", 
       x = "State")


```

So, what if I want to see what the north and south states did different? 

start with a facet_wrap using the `south` variable:

```{r}
votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2000) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(state, demVote), y = demVote)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ south) + 
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2000 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)",
       x = "State")

```

Okay, that's not great. Lets *color* by south instead.

```{r}
## I use fill instead of color here cause it looks nicer
votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2000) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(state, demVote), y = demVote, fill = south)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2000 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)",
       x = "State")

```

I'm a good data scientist, so I want my plot to have a name! and my axes to have lables! Use `labs` to add a title, subtitle, and x and y labels.

```{r}
## i've already been doing this... 
votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2000) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(state, demVote), y = demVote, fill = south)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2000 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)",
       x = "State")


```

You can move the legend with `theme(legend.position = "bottom")`

```{r, eval = T}

votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2000) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(state, demVote), y = demVote, fill = south)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2000 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)",
       x = "State",
       fill = "Southern State:") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

What else could we facet by? years! Let's filter to year in 2008 and 2016, then facet by years.

```{r}
votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2008 | year == 2016) |> 
    # this could also be year %in% c(2008, 2016)
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(state, demVote), y = demVote, fill = south)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_flip() + 
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2008 and 2016 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)",
       x = "State",
       fill = "Southern State:") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

## this reorder is weird because it's reordering on overall total, since the axes need to match. 
```

We need to know who won! We could add a vertical line at 50 for who got more, to indicate the majority of votes. Adding the layer `geom_hline()` adds a horizontal line. (What do you guess `geom_vline()` would do?)

```{r}
votedata |> 
  filter(year == 2008 | year == 2016) |> 
    # this could also be year %in% c(2008, 2016)
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(state, demVote), y = demVote, fill = south)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50) + 
    ## NOTE: this is weird because of the coordinate flip
  coord_flip() + 
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(title = "Democratic Percent of Votes by State", 
       subtitle = "For the 2008 and 2016 Presidental Election",
       y = "Dem Vote (%)",
       x = "State",
       fill = "Southern State:") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

### Getting fancy with a map!

When using geom_polygon or geom_map, you will typically need two data frames:

-   one contains the coordinates of each polygon (positions)
-   the other the values associated with each polygon (values).

An id variable links the two together. 

Run the below example code to get map graphs for votes in 2008 and then 2016. 

```{r}
library(maps)
votedata$state <- tolower(votedata$state)  ## states need to be lowercase for linking

states_map <- map_data("state") ## this gives us the lat and long for each point of each state.
  
map_plot <-  ggplot(data =  votedata %>% filter(year == 2008), aes(map_id = state)) +
    geom_map(aes(fill = demVote), map = states_map) +
    expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat)

map_plot  
```

```{r}
map_plot <-  ggplot(data =  votedata %>% filter(year == 2016), aes(map_id = state)) +
  geom_map(aes(fill = demVote), map = states_map)+
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat)

map_plot  
## turns out wyoming(?) is missing data for 2016! 
```

What if I want a map that shows which of the states are "south"? What do I change?

```{r}
map_plot_states <-  ggplot(data =  votedata %>% filter(year == 2008), 
                           aes(map_id = state)) +
  geom_map(aes(fill = south), map = states_map) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat)

map_plot_states 
## changing to 2008 so we fill that gap in, and the year doesn't matter for this
```


### Some more dplyr practice

I want to know the average democratic vote for N vs S, by year.

First, find the average democratic votes for the north and the south, every year. You'll need to do a *double* `group_by()` here. You do it in one call of the function.  

```{r}
votedata |> 
  group_by(year, south) |> 
  summarise(avg_dem_vote = mean(demVote))

```

Then, let's plot that! Pipe the result of your group_by and summarize to ggplot and geom_line(), with year on the x axis and your summarized value on the y axis. Color by the `south` variable. 

```{r}
votedata |> 
  group_by(year, south) |> 
  summarise(avg_dem_vote = mean(demVote),
            .groups = "drop_last") |> 
    ## dropping the groups to get rid of a warning
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = avg_dem_vote, color = south)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Percent Dem Vote by Year", subtitle = "Divided by North/South")


```



## More Practice with Penguins 

If you've made it all the way down here, here are a few extra prompts to try out: 

-   Count the number of male and female penguins for each species.
-   Find the average penguin mass for each island
-   Find the average bill length by sex
-   Make a plot of bill_length and bill_depth, but only for the female penguins.
-   Make a plot of flipper length and body mass, faceted by island and colored by species.
-   Plot the density of the flipper length, colored by sex
-   Plot the density of the body mass, colored by year

<or, make your own similar graphs with any of the data we've used in class so far!>

```{r}
## a selection of these

# Count the number of male and female penguins for each species.
penguins |> summarise(num_peng = n(), .by = c(species, sex))
## OR 
penguins |> group_by(species, sex) |>  summarise(num_peng = n())
## i actually don't mind having the NA values counted here - it's letting us know how many are missing info on sex for each species.

# Find the average penguin mass for each island
penguins |> 
  drop_na(body_mass_g) |> # need to remove NA here to compute averages
  group_by(island) |> 
  summarise(avg_mass = mean(body_mass_g))

# Make a plot of flipper length and body mass, faceted by island and colored by species.
penguins |> 
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>  ## doesn't change graph, just removes the warning
  ggplot(aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, colour = species)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ island)

# Plot the density of the body mass, colored by year
penguins |> 
  drop_na(body_mass_g) |> 
  ggplot(aes(body_mass_g, fill = factor(year, ordered = T))) +
    ## you have to turn year into a factor to color the densities discretely! 
    ## i ordered the factor, since they do go in order, but that's not necessary
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(fill = "Year", 
       title = "Density of Penguin Body Mass, year to year comparasion")
```
